section_summary: The section finishes an English translation of Japan’s Mariners Law, covering employment contracts, pay, working hours, leave, health, compensation, enforcement, penalties, and transitional provisions. It then presents opposing 1948 assessments of Japan’s merchant fleet: American shipowners urge caution over rebuilding it to its prewar size, while a U.S. mission in Tokyo argues that substantial coastwise and overseas capacity is needed for economic recovery.

subfiles.title: Mariners Law, concluding pages of English translation
subfiles.about: English text of Japan’s Mariners Law from employment conditions through its supplementary provisions and appended compensation schedule.
subfiles.summary: These pages regulate mariners’ contracts, wages, work hours, manning, paid holidays, food, health, employment of minors and women, and compensation for injury or death. Later chapters establish working regulations, inspection and complaint procedures, penalties, and transitional rules. Pages 234–235 contain two impressions of the appended physical-disability compensation list.

subfiles.title: Mariners Law, opening page of another copy
subfiles.about: Opening definitions and scope provisions of the Mariners Law.
subfiles.summary: Defines mariners, seamen, reservists, officers, ratings, wages, work hours, and covered shipowners.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding shipping industry petition
subfiles.about: Bailey forwards the federation’s petition opposing immediate restoration of the Japanese merchant marine to its 1930–1934 size.
subfiles.summary: Bailey says member companies are concerned about proposed Japanese fleet restoration and encloses their views submitted to the Army.

subfiles.title: Federation petition on the Japanese merchant marine
subfiles.from: Frazer A. Bailey, National Federation of American Shipping
subfiles.to: William H. Draper Jr., Assistant Secretary of the Army
subfiles.about: American shipowners ask that rebuilding Japan’s merchant fleet to approximately four million gross tons be deferred.
subfiles.summary: The federation argues that Japan’s future trade and shipping needs cannot reliably be inferred from its 1930–1934 fleet. It disputes the economic importance attributed to Japanese shipping receipts, cites past subsidies, and warns that a rapid restoration could harm American shipping. It favors Japanese domestic and nearby regional services and asks for further opportunity to present its views before policy is settled.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 655
subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum highlights the Tokyo mission’s argument for a larger Japanese merchant fleet.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the despatch’s estimate of four million gross tons, including 2.5 million tons for overseas services.

subfiles.title: Tokyo despatch No. 655 on Japan’s need for an overseas merchant marine
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The Tokyo mission argues that proposed tonnage limits would obstruct Japan’s economic recovery and overseas shipping.
subfiles.summary: The mission says foreign freight charges substantially increase Japan’s raw-material costs and drain foreign exchange. It discusses export competitiveness, possible carriage of U.S.-funded relief supplies, and the need to shift bulk domestic cargo from rail back to coastal vessels. It estimates a minimum of four million gross tons of merchant shipping, including about 2.5 million tons for foreign routes. The despatch continues beyond page 255.
